title: Electricity
blurb: Roughly one paper question in eight. Almost always includes a circuit calculation with V = I × R, plus a practical about plotting results.

items.q: State the formula linking voltage, current and resistance.
a: voltage = current × resistance
(V = I × R)
items.tip: The most-asked single question in the electricity chapter. Learn the triangle: V on top, I and R underneath.

items.q: State the formula linking power, current and voltage.
a: power = current × voltage
(P = I × V)
items.tip: The alternative form P = I²R is also on the specification and is worth knowing for power-loss-in-cables questions.

items.q: State the formula linking charge (transferred), current and time.
a: charge = current × time
(Q = I × t)
items.tip: Time must be in seconds. Charge is in coulombs (C).

items.q: State what is meant by the term electric current / voltage / power.
items.rx: meant by the term (electric current|voltage|power|direct current)
a: Current: the rate of flow of (electric) charge - the charge passing a point each second;
Voltage (potential difference): the energy transferred per unit charge (per coulomb) passing between two points;
Power: the rate of energy transfer - the energy transferred each second.
items.tip: Every one of these definitions is 'something per something'. Say the per, and the mark is yours.

items.q: Calculate the voltage across the resistor / thermistor / LDR in the circuit.
a: In series the current is the same everywhere, so find the current first if it is not given;
use V = I × R for the component asked about;
or use the fact that the voltages across series components add up to the supply voltage;
evaluate and give the unit (V).
items.tip: For a potential divider, the bigger resistance always takes the bigger share of the voltage. Use that to sanity-check your answer.

items.q: Calculate the charge transferred / the current in the circuit.
a: Select the correct formula (Q = I × t, or I = V ÷ R);
substitute the values with time converted to seconds;
evaluate and give the unit.

items.q: Draw a voltmeter on the diagram to measure the voltage across the resistor.
a: The voltmeter symbol is a circle with a V inside;
it must be drawn in parallel, connected across the two ends of that component only.
items.tip: Ammeters go in series, voltmeters go in parallel. Draw the connecting wires clearly touching the circuit.

items.q: Draw a circuit diagram the student could use for this investigation.
a: A cell or battery and the component under test connected in a complete series loop;
an ammeter in series with the component;
a voltmeter in parallel across the component;
a variable resistor (or variable supply) to change the current.
items.tip: Use correct standard symbols and make sure the circuit is closed with no gaps. A stray line loses the mark.

items.q: Explain how an object becomes positively or negatively charged by friction.
a: Friction (rubbing) transfers electrons from the cloth to the other object;
the cloth loses electrons;
so it has more protons than electrons, giving it an overall positive charge.
items.tip: Only electrons ever move. Never write that protons or 'positive charges' were transferred - that is an automatic loss of the mark.

items.q: Explain why the ammeter shows a current for a short time and then shows zero.
items.rx: ammeter shows a current for a short time
a: Electrons flow to (or from) the charged object through the circuit;
this movement of charge is a current;
the charge is neutralised / the objects reach the same potential, so there is no longer a potential difference and the current stops.

items.q: Explain how the resistance of an LDR / thermistor changes.
a: LDR: as the light intensity increases, the resistance decreases;
Thermistor: as the temperature increases, the resistance decreases;
so in a series circuit the voltage across it falls and the current in the circuit rises.
items.tip: Both go down when their input goes up. Used in light-sensing and temperature-sensing circuits.

items.q: Explain the purpose of the earth wire and the fuse, and choose a suitable fuse rating.
a: If a fault connects the live wire to the metal case, the earth wire provides a low-resistance path to the ground;
a large current flows, which melts (blows) the fuse;
this disconnects the live wire, so the case cannot give the user an electric shock;
double insulation means the appliance has a plastic case, so no earth wire is needed.
items.tip: The fuse must be in the live wire. Its rating should be just above the normal operating current of the appliance.

items.q: Give a reason why the components are connected in series / in parallel.
a: Series: one loop, so the current is the same through every component and the supply voltage is shared between them;
Parallel: separate branches, so each branch receives the full supply voltage and the current splits between the branches;
adding resistors in series increases the total resistance; adding them in parallel decreases it.
items.tip: Household lamps are wired in parallel so each gets the full mains voltage and can be switched independently.
